note: Identical to baseline-v1, re-run to measure run-to-run variance. No code, prompt or benchmark change.

cases.title: Cancelled short-notice flight, crew shortage
cases.rationale: Cancellation due to crew duty-hour shortage (carrier-controlled, S3.2b) with 3-day notice qualifies for Band B compensation: 420 units at 100% per S4.2, as no re-routing was offered. All evidence requirements met; passenger should submit formal claim to Meridian Air.

cases.title: Weather cancellation with overnight duty of care
cases.rationale: Flight cancelled due to extraordinary weather circumstances (S3.3(a)); compensation not payable under S3.1. Duty of care is owed regardless of cause (S6.1), and passenger submitted itemised receipts totalling 240 units (hotel 190 + meals 50) within the 300-unit cap. Carrier's rejection is validly challengeable under S9.1(e) for failing to separately address duty-of-care reimbursement.

cases.title: Unforeseen technical fault, six-hour delay, long haul
cases.rationale: Passenger held a confirmed booking, boarded, and arrived 6h06m late at final destination (Nairobi), qualifying under S2.1(b). The delay was caused by an unscheduled technical fault found and repaired by the carrier's own line maintenance—a carrier-controlled cause under S3.2(a), not an extraordinary event per S3.3(g), since no manufacturer/regulator airworthiness directive was issued. The 6,635 km distance places this in band C (750 units); since delay exceeds 5 hours, full compensation is payable without reduction under S5.4.

cases.title: Missed connection on one booking, tapered delay
cases.rationale: Passenger held confirmed booking on both MT119 and MT402 under single reference MT5590 and boarded MT119. The operational record (S3.6 authority) shows MT119's 2h 35m delay was caused by carrier-controlled ground handling shortfall at origin, not extraordinary circumstances. Passenger was rebooked onto MT404 and arrived at final destination SYD 4h 10m late, qualifying under S2.1(b). Band C applies (17,680 km exceeds 4,000 km): 750 units. Delay taper applies (4h 10m is ≥3h30m but <5 hours per S5.4): 750 × 50% = 375 units. No notice reduction applies to delays (S4.6). Claim should be submitted to Meridian Transcontinental.

cases.title: Missed connection across two separate bookings
cases.rationale: The delay on JJ88 to final destination FRA was 55 minutes, falling well short of the S2.1(b) threshold of 3 hours 30 minutes. The missed connection on separate booking TT4419 is not a qualifying disruption under S2.3, which permits missed-connection claims only where all segments were sold under a single booking reference. No compensation or duty of care is payable.

cases.title: Twelve days notice with a compliant re-routing offer
cases.rationale: Flight cancelled (S2.1(a)) by commercial consolidation (S3.2(d), carrier-controlled) with 12 days notice. Carrier offered re-routing departing 08:00 (1 hour before 09:00) and arriving 16:00 (3.5 hours after 12:30), satisfying S4.3 exemption. No compensation payable.

cases.title: Fourteen days notice, non-compliant re-route, exact band boundary
cases.rationale: Flight ZR260 was cancelled for a carrier-controlled cause—the carrier's own IT system failure (crew rostering system)—under S3.2(c). Notified 14 days before departure, the claim falls in the 7–20 day band, attracting 50% of the Part 5 amount (S4.2). The re-routing exemption does not apply because the replacement flight arrives 5 hours 20 minutes late, exceeding the 4-hour threshold in S4.3. At 1,200 km exactly, S5.3 assigns Band A (180 units), reduced to 90 units after the Part 4 reduction. No duty of care or downgrade evidence is in the file.

cases.title: Cancellation with twenty-five days notice
cases.rationale: The flight qualifies as a cancellation under S2.1(a) with confirmed booking. The carrier issued 26 days' notice (16 Nov to 12 Dec), exceeding the 21-day threshold in S4.2, which results in zero compensation. Duty of care is owed under S6.1 for all disruptions, but no receipts have been claimed and the passenger received a full refund, so no duty-of-care reimbursement is payable.

cases.title: Delay claim with no arrival-time evidence
cases.rationale: The booking is in scope (S1.2: confirmed booking, passenger boarded at 13:44Z, claim filed within 18 months). The cause is carrier-controlled under S3.2(a): hydraulic pump replacement by Nordfly line maintenance is an unforeseen technical fault. However, the passenger claims 4–5 hours late arrival but has no proof of actual landing time. S8.1(c) mandates evidence of actual arrival time at DOH for any S2.1(b) claim. The operational record explicitly notes 'Arrival record for this rotation not attached.' Request the actual DOH landing timestamp from 22 May 2026 to determine qualification and calculate compensation.

cases.title: Cancellation with no notification timestamp
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope (confirmed booking, flight cancelled before check-in, filed within 18 months). The disruption qualifies as a cancellation under S2.1(a), with a carrier-controlled cause (crew sickness, S3.2(b)). However, S8.1(e) requires the carrier's cancellation notification with timestamp to apply the Part 4 notice ladder. The passenger's unsubstantiated recall (6–7 Feb, email deleted) does not meet the standard. Per S8.2, the correct action is to request evidence, not to assume or reject.

cases.title: Contradictory arrival times across three documents
cases.rationale: Claim is in scope with carrier-controlled cause (APU replacement by WS line maintenance under S3.2(a)). However, a material contradiction exists on the actual arrival time—the carrier reports 16:00 (1h55m delay, does not qualify) while the passenger's photograph shows 19:40 (5h35m delay, qualifies). The operational record on-blocks field is corrupted. Per S8.2, this contradiction must be resolved before eligibility can be determined.

cases.title: Rejection citing weather contradicted by the operational record
cases.rationale: The carrier rejected the claim citing adverse weather (extraordinary), but the operational record shows the cancellation was due to crew timing out after an HB-controlled rotation delay, with no adverse weather. Per S3.6, the operational record governs, making this carrier-controlled under S3.2(b). At 2,750 km, Band B applies (420 units). Notice was less than 7 days with no re-routing exemption, so full compensation is due. The rejection is validly challengeable under S9.1(a).

cases.title: Rejection that is correct and must not be challenged
cases.rationale: The claim is properly in scope and the cancellation qualifies. However, the operational record (D3) and airport authority bulletin (D4) jointly confirm that Edinburgh Airport was closed to departures due to Storm Fionn exceeding aircraft crosswind limits—a weather circumstance below operating minima at the origin under S3.3(a). This is extraordinary, and S5 permits compensation only for carrier-controlled causes. The carrier's rejection is valid and should not be challenged.

cases.title: Angry passenger demanding premature escalation
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope (confirmed booking, cancelled before departure, filed within 18 months) and qualifies under S2.1(a). The 2,730 km distance places it in Band B (420 units). The cause—internal IT systems failure—is carrier-controlled under S3.2(c), attracting full compensation. Cancellation notice was given 12 hours 45 minutes before departure (less than 7 days), so 100% of 420 units is payable under S4.2. Escalation to the regulator is not yet permitted: S10.1(a) requires 56 days to elapse since filing (08 Jun); only 20 have passed as of 28 Jun. The passenger must await the carrier's response or escalate after 56 days if no substantive reply is received.

cases.title: Challenge ignored for thirty-five days, escalation ripe
cases.rationale: Claim is in scope with 7h 42m final-destination delay qualifying under S2.1(b). The operational record (S3.6-governing) shows Altair's own maintenance found the technical fault—carrier-controlled, not extraordinary. At 7,930 km, Band C applies: 750 units. Escalation is now warranted: 35 days have elapsed since the valid challenge on 18 Mar, exceeding S10.1(b)'s 28-day response window.

cases.title: Partial settlement: duty of care paid, compensation wrongly refused
cases.rationale: The operational record (D3) shows the cancellation was caused by a carrier IT system failure (crew-rostering and dispatch platform outage), not weather as the carrier claims. Per S3.6, the operational record governs; this is carrier-controlled under S3.2(c), making the claim eligible for full compensation of 420 units (Band B, 2,900 km). The carrier's rejection is invalid under S9.1(a) and should be challenged; the passenger's full entitlement is 720 units (420 compensation + 300 duty of care already paid), not just the 300 offered.

cases.title: Involuntary downgrade with no delay and no cancellation
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope with sufficient evidence (confirmed booking, boarding pass, and clear downgrade). However, a downgrade is not a Part 2 qualifying disruption (the flight arrived on time with no delay, and was neither cancelled nor fully denied boarding), so Part 5 compensation under the long-haul band is not payable. Under Part 7, the passenger is entitled to 40% reimbursement of the fare paid for the affected segment: 40% × 800 = 320 units. The passenger should submit this Part 7 claim to the carrier.

cases.title: Extraordinary cause with forty hours to recover

derivation: S2.1(a) cancellation
S3.3(e) the bird strike is itself an extraordinary cause
S3.5 the extraordinary event ended 22 Jun 01:10Z and scheduled departure was 23 Jun 17:10Z, roughly 40 hours later
S3.5 more than 12 hours elapsed, and spare airframes were available, so the cause reverts to carrier-controlled
S4.1 notice 22 Jun 23:40 -> 23 Jun 17:10Z is under 7 days -> 100%
S4.4 no re-routing offered -> no exemption
S5.1 2,190 km -> band B -> 420 units

cases.title: Fleet-wide airworthiness directive, duty of care only
cases.rationale: Flight cancelled due to extraordinary manufacturer-notified airworthiness defect (S3.3(g)), so no Part 5 compensation is payable under S3.1. However, duty of care is owed regardless of cause (S6.1), and the passenger's itemised receipts (hotel 140 units, meals 40 units) are fully substantiated and within the 300-unit cap. The passenger should submit a formal claim to the carrier for 180 units of duty-of-care reimbursement.

cases.title: Passenger overstates the delay; evidence shows just under threshold
cases.rationale: The passenger's arrival at the final destination was 3 hours 20 minutes late, which falls short of the 3 hours 30 minutes threshold in S2.1(b) required for a qualifying disruption. Without a qualifying disruption under Part 2, no compensation under Part 5 or duty of care under Part 6 is payable, regardless of the carrier-controlled cause (crew delay under S3.2(b)).

cases.title: Decisive fact buried at document eight of nine
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and the flight was cancelled (S2.1(a)) due to crew duty-limit breach (S3.2(b), carrier-controlled). Notification was given 3 days 18 hours before departure—less than 7 days, ordinarily triggering 100% Part 5 compensation (S4.2). However, the carrier offered re-routing departing 30 minutes earlier than scheduled and arriving 95 minutes later, both within the S4.4 exemption thresholds (no more than 1 hour before; less than 2 hours after). The passenger accepted. No compensation is payable. No duty of care receipts were filed. No response from the carrier is on file despite 101 days elapsed since claim (20 May to 29 August); S10.1(a) permits escalation to the Synthetic Passenger Rights Body.

cases.title: Two composed reductions at an exact band boundary
cases.rationale: The passenger held a confirmed booking, boarded EM604 (D2), and arrived 3h 45m late at final destination AMM (D3), qualifying under S2.1(b). The cause was late inbound aircraft due to EM's own engineering hold (D4), a carrier-controlled cause under S3.2(e). At exactly 4,000 km (S5.3), Band B applies: 420 units. The 3h 45m delay falls in the S5.4 taper band (≥3h30m but <5h), reducing compensation to 50%: 210 units. No Part 4 reduction applies (delays are always 100%, subject to taper). All evidence required by S8.1 is on file.

cases.title: Rejection resting on a re-routing offer that is not in the record
cases.rationale: Claim is in scope: confirmed booking (D1), flight cancelled before check-in, claim filed within 18 months. Disruption qualifies under S2.1(a). Cause is carrier-controlled: commercial consolidation under S3.2(d). Three days' notice (14 Nov 09:00 UTC to 17 Nov 15:50) triggers 100% compensation under S4.2; re-routing exemption S4.4 does not apply because no offer appears in D2 or contact history D4. Passenger was accepted for travel (CONFIRMED booking D1 satisfies S8.1(b)). Distance 4,590 km = Band C = 750 units. Rejection citing re-routing exemption is validly challengeable under S9.1(c).

cases.title: Strong claim filed nineteen months late

derivation: S1.2(c) a claim must be filed within 18 months of the scheduled departure of the first affected segment
Scheduled departure 04 Feb 2025, filing 12 Sep 2026, an elapsed 19 months and 8 days
S1.3 a claim failing any limb of S1.2 is out of scope and receives no compensation and no duty of care
The merits are strong and the carrier admits fault, and none of that survives S1.3
S2 and S3 are reached in the analysis but cannot rescue an out-of-scope claim

cases.title: Receipts with a non-reimbursable item and a cap

derivation: S2.1(a) cancellation
S3.3(b) airspace closure by the air navigation service provider, not caused by the carrier -> extraordinary
S3.5 does not apply: the closure was still in force at the scheduled departure time
No Part 5 compensation is payable
S6.1 duty of care is owed regardless of cause
S6.2(b) hotel 210.00 and airport transfer 21.00 are reimbursable
S6.2(a) meals 31.00 and 58.00 are reimbursable
Replacement clothing is not among the categories in S6.2 and is not reimbursable, so 95.00 is excluded
Reimbursable subtotal is 210 + 31 + 58 + 21 = 320.00 units
S6.3 the cap is 300 units per passenger per disruption -> 300 units payable
S6.4 itemised receipts are present for every line

cases.title: Denied boarding, four hours late, no taper

derivation: S1.2(b) the passenger was denied boarding, which satisfies the limb directly
S2.1(c) involuntary denied boarding on a confirmed booking qualifies in its own right
S3.2(d) overbooking -> carrier-controlled
S5.1 1,720 km -> band B -> 420 units
S4.6 the notice ladder does not apply to denied boarding; it is compensated at 100% subject to S5.4
S5.4 the taper is confined to claims qualifying under S2.1(b) only; this claim qualifies under S2.1(c), so the 4h 20m arrival delay does not reduce the amount
420 units payable in full

cases.title: Stated cause contradicted by the record, where the policy resolves it

derivation: S2.1(a) cancellation
S3.6 where the carrier's stated cause and the operational record disagree, the operational record governs, so this conflict is resolved by rule and is not an S8.3 evidence request
S3.2(b) crew sickness with no standby -> carrier-controlled, corroborated by D4
S4.1 notice 09 Sep 04:50 -> 09 Sep 06:40 is under 7 days -> 100%
S4.4 no re-routing offered -> no exemption
S5.1 1,450 km -> band B -> 420 units
S6.1 duty of care was owed but D6 records that nothing was incurred
D2 is a customer-service letter, not a rejection, and no claim has been filed, so the correct action is to submit rather than to challenge
S10.2 escalation would be premature

cases.title: Settlement offer that matches the full entitlement

derivation: S2.1(a) cancellation
S3.2(c) carrier's own flight-planning system outage -> carrier-controlled
S4.1 notice 06 Dec 15:05 -> 06 Dec 17:30 is under 7 days -> 100%
S4.4 the re-route arrived roughly 24 hours late, far outside the 2 hour window -> no exemption
S5.1 1,600 km -> band B -> 420 units
S6.2(a)+(b) overnight wait with meals and hotel, S6.4 receipts present, S6.3 170.00 is under the 300 cap -> 170 units
Full entitlement across Parts 5, 6 and 7 is 420 + 170 + 0 = 590.00 units
S9.4 the offer of 590.00 units meets the full entitlement and should be accepted
S9.3 does not apply because nothing is being refused
